clinicalPearls: Typically presents with mild to moderate intellectual disability and a characteristic epilepsy beginning in early childhood
Myoclonic-atonic epilepsy (Doose-like), atypical absences and generalised seizures are the usual pattern
Early development may be relatively preserved before seizure onset, followed by developmental slowing or regression
Autism spectrum features, behavioural difficulties and hypotonia are frequently present
Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SLC6A1, usually de novo and autosomal dominant, encoding the GABA transporter GAT1
EEG commonly shows generalised spike-and-wave discharges consistent with a generalised epilepsy
Movement problems such as ataxia and tremor may accompany the epilepsy
reference.pathophysiology: SLC6A1 encodes GAT1, the principal transporter that clears the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA from the synaptic cleft into neurons and astrocytes, terminating inhibitory signalling and recycling GABA. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants reduce transporter function through haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative effects, disturbing the normal spatial and temporal control of GABAergic inhibition. Dysregulated inhibitory neurotransmission destabilises cortical and thalamocortical networks, producing the generalised epilepsy, and impairs the balance of excitation and inhibition needed for normal cognitive development. The resulting picture combines myoclonic-atonic epilepsy with intellectual disability and autistic features.
additionalDifferentials: Myoclonic-atonic epilepsy (Doose syndrome) of other cause
Other genetic generalised epilepsies with intellectual disability
additionalInvestigations: EEG to characterise generalised spike-and-wave and other epileptiform activity
Brain MRI, usually normal or non-specific
Gene panel or exome sequencing including SLC6A1
Chromosomal microarray to detect deletions involving the locus
redFlags: Frequent drop attacks or myoclonic-atonic seizures causing falls
Developmental regression coinciding with seizure onset
Status epilepticus, including atypical absence status
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability with epilepsy that is variably responsive to treatment; seizures may improve over time in some. Long-term outcome depends on seizure control and cognitive impact, and management is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Diagnosing generic Doose syndrome and not testing for SLC6A1
Overlooking pre-seizure developmental concerns because early milestones seemed adequate
Assuming a normal MRI excludes a genetic epilepsy
Using vigabatrin-type strategies without recognising the underlying GABAergic transport defect
management: Control the myoclonic-atonic and absence seizures with broad-spectrum antiseizure medication such as valproate, ethosuximide or lamotrigine, avoiding agents that aggravate generalised seizures
Provide neurodevelopmental support with special education, behavioural therapy and speech and language therapy for the intellectual disability and autism features
Offer physiotherapy and occupational therapy for hypotonia and motor difficulties
Consider ketogenic dietary therapy in drug-resistant seizures
Undertake regular EEG monitoring and review of seizure control over time
Offer genetic counselling for the usually de novo autosomal dominant variant, with parental testing and recurrence-risk advice, within multidisciplinary paediatric neurology follow-up
